name: fast-containers (SIMD/hugepage B+Tree)
workload: 10M-element trees (8-byte int64 key + 32-byte or 256-byte value); mixed insert/find/erase steady-state ops timed via RDTSC, P50 and P99.9 latency reported; also tested at 10K elements
claimed_speedup: ~2.1-4.8x faster insert/find/erase (P50 and P99.9) than std::map at 10M elements across both value sizes (e.g. INSERT P99.9 1023ns vs 3587ns, FIND P99.9 864ns vs 2312ns); at 10K elements std::map becomes competitive and wins some tail-latency cases (e.g. ERASE P99.9)
compiler_and_flags: Clang, Release build (exact optimization flags not itemized)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16-core), hyperthreading disabled, core 15 isolated via kernel boot params, Linux 6.16.3
tradeoffs: Requires C++23 (GCC14+/Clang19+) and x86-64 AVX2; SIMD search paths and RDTSC timing are x86-64 specific; hugepage allocator needs OS hugepage configuration; no pointer/iterator stability guarantee like std::map; only built/tested on Linux
caveats: Single-author work-in-progress project explicitly built with heavy AI-agent assistance per README; benchmark is self-reported and not independently reproduced; which std::map/libstdc++ or libc++ variant was tested is not stated; advantage shrinks or reverses at small (10K) tree sizes

name: tlx::btree_map / btree_set / btree_multimap (STX B+Tree lineage)
workload: Random-integer insertion into trees up to ~4M items (map/set/multimap/multiset variants); average insertion speed plotted across successive STX B+Tree speedtests run in 2007, 2011 and 2013
claimed_speedup: ~2x faster average insertion than std::map/std::multiset's red-black tree for trees larger than ~1,024,000 items in the 2007 test ('red-black tree requires almost twice as much time as a B+ tree with 32 slots'); the 2011/2013 reruns show the same qualitative win but with the crossover point shifting to roughly 100,000 items
hardware: 2007: Pentium 4 3.2GHz, 2GB RAM; 2011: Intel Core i7 950 @3.07GHz; 2013: Intel Core i7 920 @2.67GHz
stars_or_usage: 458 stars (tlx); predecessor stx-btree used in academic string-sorting/Thrill research code
tradeoffs: B+tree stores keys and values in separate parallel arrays per node (different memory layout than std::map's node-per-pair); no pointer/iterator stability guarantee; pulls in the broader tlx helper-library dependency
caveats: Benchmark numbers are 12-19 years old, run on now-obsolete hardware and compilers (Pentium 4 / Core i7 9xx-series, gcc 4.x); the speedtest page belongs to the predecessor stx-btree project (marked OBSOLETE and folded into tlx) rather than the current tlx repo itself, though the B+tree code lineage is continuous; no rerun found on modern hardware/toolchains
found_via: WebSearch: tlx::btree_map "std::map" faster benchmark Bingmann (surfaced while following up the Abseil B-tree ecosystem mentioned in HN 'Fast B-Trees' thread, id=41761986)

name: S+ tree (Algorithmica static B-tree array layout)
workload: Point/predecessor lookup over sorted arrays of 32-bit integers up to 2^25 (~33.5M) elements; reciprocal-throughput microbenchmark (batched independent queries) on an AMD Zen 2 CPU with Clang 10
claimed_speedup: up to 15x faster than std::lower_bound for small (cache-resident) arrays and ~8x faster for large arrays (>1e6, per repo README); up to 30x faster than std::set lookup and ~15x faster than an Abseil B-tree with pointers, for large arrays (per article)
compiler_and_flags: Clang 10, targeting a Zen 2 CPU (exact optimization flags not itemized)
tradeoffs: Static structure: no insert/delete support without a full rebuild, so it is not a drop-in replacement for a mutable std::set; SIMD/AVX and layout choices are microarchitecture-tuned; requires branchless/permutation tricks that add code complexity
caveats: Headline speedups are reciprocal-throughput numbers from batches of independent queries; the author explicitly notes that single-query real latency (with data dependencies) shows a much smaller gain ('not that impressive'), so most of the win is instruction-level parallelism across queries rather than lower per-lookup latency; repository has no LICENSE file or stated license
found_via: Hacker News thread "Static B-Trees: A data structure for faster binary search" (id=30376140), linking to en.algorithmica.org/hpc/data-structures/s-tree/

name: boost::container::flat_set / flat_map
workload: 500,000 randomized insert+remove operations on sets of size 2 to 8192 32-bit-ish elements, comparing vector-backed boost::container::flat_set against red-black-tree std::set
claimed_speedup: flat_set ~1.1-2.5x faster than std::set for insert+remove at sizes 2-128 (largest gain at smallest size); crossover between size 128 and 256; std::set ~13.4x faster than flat_set at size 8192
compiler_and_flags: -O3 (hardware and full compiler version not stated)
stars_or_usage: 127 stars on the split boostorg/container mirror; ships as part of Boost and is used extremely widely across C++ codebases
tradeoffs: Vector-backed storage means O(n) insert/erase in the middle versus O(log n) for std::set; no pointer/iterator stability across insert/erase; best suited to small/medium or read-mostly sets, not large frequently-mutated ones
caveats: Benchmark is a single-author 2014 blog post (not the boost repo's own benchmark suite), hardware unspecified, single-run numbers with no error bars, and only covers int-like keys with a 500K insert+remove mix; the performance advantage clearly reverses for larger sets (~8K elements) in the same data
found_via: WebSearch: "boost::container::flat_map" benchmark "std::map" reddit OR hacker news speedup
